schools.summary: Keil and Delitzsch frame the whole register (begins and ends at the sheep-gate, each party building 'by the side of' the last); Ellicott sets the gate in the priests' quarter, the victims washed in the pool of Bethesda, its sanctifying an earnest of the wall's later consecration.
Matthew Henry makes the priests' precedence a lesson — ministers foremost in every good work — and reads the sanctifying as committing the city and walls to divine protection.

Clarke reads 'sanctified' as consecration of the gate through which the victims passed; Wesley grants the word can mean 'prepared/repaired' but judges dedication by prayer and sacrifice the better sense.
Gill fixes Eliashib as grandson of Jeshua, first to rise, setting a good example to priests and people.

debates.question: Does the priests' 'sanctifying' of the sheep gate mean a solemn dedication or merely to prepare and repair it?

sides.position: a true dedication by prayer and sacrifice
the word can mean only 'prepared/repaired'

schools.summary: Keil and Delitzsch parse the recurring 'next unto him' (singular or plural suffix, builders as company or individuals) and place the men of Jericho with Zaccur between the tower of Hananeel and the fish-gate; Ellicott notes the customary phrase honours the high priest and that Jericho built opposite their own city.
Gill takes the men of Jericho for the posterity of that city, building on from where the priests ended.
Henry gathers them among builders not of Jerusalem who consulted purely the public good — every Israelite lending a hand to build up Jerusalem.

themes: 'next unto him' as a map of the wall

schools.summary: Gill rehearses the disputed site (Lightfoot south, others north) and inclines west toward the Mediterranean, Tyre, and Joppa, citing Rauwolff's gate of Hebron.

Keil and Delitzsch tie the name to the fish-market (cf. Neh. 12:39; 2 Chron. 33:14; Zeph. 1:10) and place it west of the Hananeel tower; Ellicott has the fish enter from Jordan and Galilee, notes the builders' names omitted, and renders the crossbars and catches.
Clarke cautions that we know scarcely anything of these gates, all plans of Jerusalem being mere conjecture.

debates.question: Where did the fish gate stand and whence came its fish?

sides.position: westward, toward the Mediterranean (Tyre, Joppa)
in the north wall west of the Hananeel tower, fish from Jordan and Galilee

outliers.note: Stands back from all the topography: we know scarcely anything of these gates, and all plans of Jerusalem are works of conjecture, however learnedly men have written of them.

themes: the disputed topography of the gates

schools.summary: Keil and Delitzsch gloss 'repaired' as to strengthen, to make good the gaps (cf. vv.9,27), and note Meremoth's second portion at v.21 and Meshullam's standing at Neh. 6:18; Ellicott: repaired is literally strengthened, whereas the gates were 'built.'
Gill draws the distinction that the wall was only weakened, not demolished, so strengthened rather than rebuilt — a usage running through the chapter.
Henry gathers the three into his rule that every one furthers the public good to the utmost of his power — united force conquering what no single hand dares.

themes: heads of houses named for honour

schools.summary: Keil and Delitzsch read 'put not their necks to the work' as refusing the yoke of service (cf. Jer. 27:11) and note the Tekoites' second portion at v.27; Ellicott calls the verse the solitary instance of internal opposition, terming the labour 'the work of the Lord.'
Wesley probes the nobles' motive (sloth, covetousness, or secret compliance with the enemy) and turns it to a maxim: let no noble think anything beneath him by which he may serve his country.
Gill sets the Tekoites of Tekoa in Judah, repairing next to those before them.
Henry reads the nobles' disdain — as if their peerage discharged them from serving God — and marks the common Tekoites shaming their lords by a double share.

themes: the yoke of the work of the Lord

schools.summary: Gill gathers the guesses — the old gate led to old Salem, or is Lightfoot's second/third gate, or Vatablus's gate of the old pool, or the gate of the old wall in Josephus, leading north.
Ellicott: nowhere else mentioned, probably the Damascus gate, or by a conjectural repointing 'the gate of the old wall.'
Henry marks the two co-founders sharing the honour, and passes on the tradition that the gate belonged to ancient Salem, first built by Melchizedek.

sides.position: the gate of ancient Salem (Melchizedek's city), or of the old pool
the Damascus gate, or 'the gate of the old wall' by a repointing

schools.summary: Keil and Delitzsch make Melatiah and Jadon superintendents of the Gibeon and Mizpah men (Meronoth near Mizpah, cf. 1 Chron. 27:30; Mizpah = Nebi Samwil, cf. Josh. 19:26) and read 'unto the throne' as marking men of the Pechah's jurisdiction beyond the river; Ellicott makes it the pechah's residence at Jerusalem.
Clarke takes the throne for the governor's house of justice, noting Jerusalem's earlier Persian deputy (Neh. 5:15); Wesley, the palace or throne the governor beyond Euphrates sometimes kept.
Gill sets Gibeon and Mizpah both in Benjamin, one man of each.
Henry gathers these with the men of Jericho as builders not of Jerusalem who consulted purely the public good.

debates.question: What is 'the throne of the governor on this side the river'?

sides.position: a description of the builders' allegiance — men under the Pechah's jurisdiction beyond the river
a physical seat or residence of the Persian governor at Jerusalem

schools.summary: Keil and Delitzsch take the 'broad wall' for a length between the tower of the furnaces and the gate of Ephraim (Neh. 12:38); Ellicott reads the verb literally as 'left' — they left a sound stretch untouched — and marks the unexplained silence about the gate of Ephraim (Neh. 12:39).

Clarke notes goldsmiths, apothecaries, and merchants formed guilds, the apothecaries dealing in spices for temple incense; Wesley keeps 'fortified,' either because less demolished or to mark extraordinary care in making it stronger than ever.
Gill names Uzziel of the goldsmiths (the Tzorephim) and Hananiah of the apothecaries' guild.
Henry honours the tradesmen who did not plead their callings but trusted God to make up what they lost by leaving their shops.

debates.question: Does the verb mean they 'fortified' the wall or 'left' a sound stretch untouched?

sides.position: 'left' — a portion needing no restoration passed over (with the gate of Ephraim in it)
'fortified' — repaired and made stronger than before

themes: the silence about the gate of Ephraim

schools.summary: Clarke divides the city into a Judah part and a Benjamin part, each with its governor (Rephaiah and Shallum of v.12); Wesley likens it to Rome's regions, two rulers under the chief governor.
Gill takes 'half part of Jerusalem' of the city divided between Judah and Benjamin, Rephaiah a governor of the Judah part.
Keil and Delitzsch dissent — the 'half part' is the rural district belonging to Jerusalem (cf. vv.15,19), not half the town — and leave Hattush's identity open (cf. Neh. 10:5; Ezra 8:2).
Henry: rulers thought themselves bound in honour to build, called rulers of but 'a part' because the Persians set two as a watch on each other.

debates.question: Does 'the half part of Jerusalem' mean half the city or a district belonging to it?

sides.position: half the city itself, cloven between Judah and Benjamin, each with a governor
the rural district belonging to Jerusalem

themes: a watch set on each other

schools.summary: Keil and Delitzsch trace the sequence to Malchijah and Hashub (Zerubbabel's houses, Ezra 2:6,32) and, with Bertheau, own that 'the other piece' without a named first portion may betray a gap in the text (a lost notice of the gate of Ephraim before v.8).
Gill: Jedaiah repaired the wall right against his house, likely with special care for his own safety.
Henry makes the recurring 'over against his house' a rule — if every one mend one, we shall all be mended; if he that has but a chamber repair before it, he does his part.

themes: each mending the length before his door
a possible gap in the text
the safety of the whole from each one's care

schools.summary: Ellicott checks the assumption behind 'the other piece' — it often marks not a builder's second portion but simply 'a second measure' along the wall, where no first piece is named.
Clarke reads 'the other piece' as that left by Jedaiah after repairing opposite his house, and guesses the principal people were obliged to repair opposite their own dwellings.
Gill notes the fathers of Malchijah and Hashub were heads of families that came out of captivity with Zerubbabel.
Henry's rule covers them — each furthering the public good to the utmost of his power, here rebuilding the tower of the furnaces.

debates.question: What does 'the other piece' mean here?

sides.position: a genuine second portion — the length Jedaiah left after his own house
merely 'a second measure' along the wall, with no first portion implied

themes: labouring to the utmost of one's power

schools.summary: Keil and Delitzsch fix the pronoun on Shallum himself, not a district whose 'daughters' would be villages; Ellicott sets aside the villages reading as needless — the women of Jerusalem might do voluntarily what they were not pressed to do.
Wesley makes the daughters heiresses or rich widows who bore part of the charge; Clarke glosses Shallum as 'son of the Enchanter,' ruler of the other half part (cf. v.9).
Gill gives Shallum's name as serpent-charmer or wise counsellor (from Ben Melech).
Henry dwells on the ladies helping the work with money for materials and wages, recalling the women who laboured with Paul in the gospel (Phil. 4:3).

sides.position: his literal daughters — women (heiresses or widows) helping with means or hands
the villages of the district he governed

themes: the breadth of the willing spirit

schools.summary: Keil and Delitzsch place the valley-gate in the west near the Jaffa gate, make Hanun ruler of Zanoah (now Zanna, cf. Josh. 15:34), and keep the 'thousand cubits' under the verb of repairing; Ellicott reads the thousand cubits as strengthened not built, a wide space less damaged.
Clarke sets Zanoah in Judah (Josh. 15:34).
Gill names Hanun and the inhabitants of Zanoah as the builders of the valley gate.
Henry counts the men of Zanoah among builders not of Jerusalem who served the public good.
Ellicott: 'son of Rechab' does not mean a Rechabite but names the father, 'part of Beth-haccerem' the district around; Keil and Delitzsch carry the dung gate on to the fountain gate.
Clarke places Beth-haccerem in Benjamin (Jer. 6:1); Wesley takes it for a town whose government was divided between two persons.
Gill weighs whether Malchiah was a Rechabite (who might build walls though not houses) but thinks it more probable he was not of that family.
Henry gathers the rulers of 'a part' — the Persians setting two over each city — among whom Malchiah of Beth-haccerem came to build even the gate of dung.

debates.question: Was Malchiah 'the son of Rechab' a Rechabite?

sides.position: perhaps a Rechabite (who might build walls though forbidden houses), but more likely not
not a Rechabite at all — 'son of Rechab' simply names his father

themes: son of Rechab, not a Rechabite
care even for the humblest gate

schools.summary: Keil and Delitzsch give Shallun of the district of Mizpah, gloss 'covered it' as roofing with beams (cf. vv.3,6), and fix the gate by the pool of Shelach/Siloah at the king's garden; Ellicott adds the pool (the 'king's pool') fed by a subterranean conduit and the stairs on the flank of Ophel, owning the course now hard to trace.
Clarke identifies Siloah with the pool of the gospels and explains the stairs of the city of David by Jerusalem's uneven ground, like the stepped streets of Bristol.
Gill names the gate of the fountain and its builder.

themes: the pool of Siloah and the king's garden
the stairs of the city of David
the course grown hard to trace

schools.summary: Keil and Delitzsch note the shift to 'after him' and set Nehemiah of Beth-zur's wall opposite the sepulchres of the house of David (cf. 2 Chron. 32:33); Ellicott makes the pool Hezekiah's (Isa. 22:11) and the house of the mighty David's elect troops (1 Chron. 11:10).

Clarke (with Calmet) takes the pool for Hezekiah's siege-reservoir (2 Chron. 32:4) and the house of the mighty for a guard-post; Wesley makes the pool Hezekiah's (2 Kings 20:20), the house of the valiant a lodging for the king's captains.
Gill sets Beth-zur as a strong fortified place in Judah.
Henry marks this Nehemiah a namesake of the governor, and asks whether the governor built no piece — answering that he did more than any, overseeing all and keeping watch (Neh. 4:16).

themes: the governor's namesake and his oversight

schools.summary: Keil and Delitzsch set the Levites in order (Rehum, then Hashabiah ruler of half Keilah 'in his part') and carry on to the armoury at the turning (v.19); Ellicott marks the circuit coming round to the Temple and the other half of Keilah (now Kila) in the next verse.
Gill names Rehum the son of Bani as one of the Levites.
Henry's pattern of divided rule — two rulers of Keilah as a watch on each other — presides over the verse.

themes: the circuit turning to the Temple
every rank of the people building

schools.summary: Keil and Delitzsch name the head of the second half, Bavai the son of Henadad, ruler of the other half part of Keilah, joining the two halves of the town on neighbouring lengths.
Gill takes 'their brethren' for the brethren of the two named, or (with Jarchi) the Levites their brethren in general.
Henry: rulers of but 'the half part,' the Persians appointing two as a watch on each other, as Rome had two consuls.

themes: brother beside brother on the wall

schools.summary: Keil and Delitzsch read the 'armoury of the angle' (an abbreviation of arsenal) on the east side of Zion where the wall formed an angle; Ellicott sets it at the north-west corner of the city of David with its own wall.
Clarke takes the going up to the armoury for a tower guarding the angle, or the city arsenal where weapons were kept to arm the people in danger.
Gill sets Ezer over another Mizpah or the other half of it.

themes: the course hard to trace here

schools.summary: Keil and Delitzsch reject Bertheau's emendation 'up the hill' and take the rare word as 'emulously' (cf. Jer. 22:15; 12:5); Ellicott owns the reason of Baruch's emulation near the high priest's house does not appear.
Clarke: Baruch distinguished himself by zeal and activity; Wesley: eminent diligence and fervency, provoking many to greater pains.
Gill reads 'earnestly' as 'in anger' — angry at the backwardness shown, and so working with all haste.
Henry: Baruch repaired with an inflamed zeal, the most vigorous of any, and his example quickened his neighbours.

debates.question: What does the rare word describing Baruch's repair mean?

sides.position: 'in anger' — a holy indignation at others' backwardness
'emulously/earnestly' — a generous rivalry to excel
an emendation, 'up the hill' (rejected)

schools.summary: Keil and Delitzsch confirm Meremoth's second portion and read the following priests as men of the Jordan valley (kikkar, cf. Neh. 12:28; Gen. 13:10); Ellicott: Meremoth added the wall under the high priest's house to his earlier labour.
Wesley notes the door was at one end of the house, not the middle as now.
Gill: having finished his first part (v.4), Meremoth sets his hand a second time to the work.
Henry: some who had first done helped their fellows and took another share — Meremoth (vv.4,21) and the Tekoites (vv.5,27).

themes: the length by the high priest's house

schools.summary: Ellicott reads 'the men of the plain' as priests dwelling in the Jordan valley, the Kikkar of Scripture.
Clarke sets them in the country about Jerusalem, where the temple singers and priests dwelt (Neh. 12:28).
Gill allows either — the plain of Jericho, a later priests' station, or the plain about Jerusalem.
Henry gathers them among those active in the work who were not inhabitants of Jerusalem and so consulted purely the public good.

debates.question: Where is 'the plain' whose priests these were?

sides.position: the Jordan valley (the Kikkar), near Jericho
the level country and villages about Jerusalem
either — Jericho's plain or Jerusalem's

themes: the Jordan valley or about Jerusalem
no Israelite absent from the work

schools.summary: Keil and Delitzsch set Benjamin, Hashub, and Azariah over against their houses (little else known) and carry on to Binnui at the turning of the wall.
Gill joins the 'after him' to the last of the priests just named.
Henry repeats his rule (cf. v.10) — each applying himself to the part nearest him; if every one mend one, we shall all be mended.

themes: the city knit together for its own defence
private care raising the public wall

schools.summary: Keil and Delitzsch trace Binnui's second portion to the turning and the corner, join 'high' to the tower (not the king's house), and note the same tower called 'great' at v.27; Ellicott fixes the corner as the north-eastern angle of the city of David.
Gill: Binnui began where Azariah ended.
Henry's rule — every one taking his share, more or less by his ability, and minding it — covers the hard angle of the king's house.

themes: the high tower by the king's house
the north-eastern angle of David's city
the record faithful to hard ground

schools.summary: Keil and Delitzsch set Palal opposite the tower projecting from the king's high house by the prison-court and Pedaiah after him, then the Nethinim of Ophel to the water-gate east (Neh. 12:37); Ellicott renders 'the high tower outlying from the king's palace' and notes the prison-gate hard by (Neh. 12:39).
Gill: Palal dwelt over against the turning and repaired what stood against him.
Henry's reflection — every one minding the share that fell to him, some at the great public works — bears on the palace quarter.

themes: the king's high house and its tower
the wall through the royal quarter

schools.summary: Ellicott sets aside the Syriac's inserted 'who,' describes Ophel as the spur south of the Temple where the temple-servants dwelt apart (water-gate east to the king's tower west), and notes nothing is said of their part in the labour; Keil and Delitzsch reach the place where the wall encloses Ophel.
Gill takes the Nethinim, servants to the Levites, to have repaired here where their dwellings were.

debates.question: Does the verse make the Nethinim builders here, or only mark where they dwelt?

sides.position: they repaired the wall by their own dwellings
the text records only their dwelling — nothing is said of their part in the labour

themes: the settled order of the restored city

schools.summary: Keil and Delitzsch fix the Tekoites' second piece from the great tower to the wall of Ophel, much built on by Jotham (2 Chron. 27:3) and Manasseh (2 Chron. 33:14); Ellicott corrects 'after them' to 'after him,' referring to Pedaiah of v.25.
Wesley: the Tekoites, done with their first share sooner, freely supplied others' defects — their double diligence noted for their nobles' shame and their own honour.
Gill: their zeal shines the brighter because their nobles were so backward (cf. v.5).
Henry: their nobles' bad example, instead of excusing them, made them the more forward to double work, to shame or atone for their lords' carelessness.

Keil and Delitzsch place the horse gate near the temple and palace (2 Chron. 23:15; 2 Kings 11:6; Jer. 31:40), in the wall over the Tyropoean valley; Ellicott sets it between Temple and palace, the space from Ophel needing no repair.
Clarke: the gate where horses passed to water, near the temple, whence one rode no farther toward it — horses never plentiful in Jerusalem.
Gill gives the accounts of the name — stables, watering at Kidron, or Josephus's horse tower.

themes: the ministers girding their own house

schools.summary: Keil and Delitzsch make Zadok head of the priestly order of Immer (Ezra 2:37) and hold Shemaiah the keeper of the east gate hardly the same as the Davidic Shemaiah of 1 Chron. 3:22, the east gate being the temple's, not the water-gate of v.26; Ellicott simply marks the coincidence of the name (1 Chron. 3:22).
Gill: Zadok, perhaps a man of note with a large house, repaired over against it.

themes: Zadok of the house of Immer
the keeper of the east gate
office and labour in one place

schools.summary: Keil and Delitzsch name the builders and distinguish this Meshullam from the man of v.4 (there marked 'son of Meshezabeel'), glossing the rare word for his 'chamber' or dwelling (cf. Neh. 13:7).
Wesley draws the lesson from Hanun the sixth son — his five elder brethren laid not their hands to the work, yet in doing good we need not stay for our betters to go before us.
Gill: of Zalaph's six sons only the youngest wrought, noted to his commendation.
Henry honours the younger who outdid his elders and the lodger who repaired before his single chamber — the most honourable are the most useful.

Keil and Delitzsch read 'goldsmith's son' as a guild-member and keep the Masoretic division of the obscure clause against the LXX/Bertheau; Ellicott makes it 'the house of the Nethinim,' ties the merchants (dove-sellers) to the temple-servants, and owns the gate Miphkad unknown.
Gill: Malchiah, son of Tzoreph, named from the goldsmith's trade.
Henry: honest tradesmen, goldsmiths and merchants, active in the work at the last as at the first.

debates.question: How is the obscure clause to be divided?

sides.position: Masoretic — Malchiah repaired the whole to the corner
LXX — Malchiah to the house of the Nethinim, the merchants opposite the gate Miphkad

themes: the house of the Nethinim and the merchants

schools.summary: Keil and Delitzsch close the east wall at the sheep-gate where the description began (v.1), judge it less damaged, and survey the whole as forty-two sections without a single gap; Ellicott: the goldsmiths and merchants filled the small space to complete the circuit.
Clarke discusses 'goldsmiths' (workers in metal, generally gold) as a corporate guild and the varying old versions of the two trades.
Gill marks the place where the building first began and now ended.
Henry: the work so divided that every one knew and minded his task, without strife save to do most for the public good, no gap left in the end.

themes: ending where it began, at the sheep gate
